\]

Given the density matrix:
\[

\]
We can express \(\left|0\right\rangle \left\langle 0\right|\) and \(\left|1\right\rangle \left\langle 1\right|\) in matrix form:
\[

\left|1\right\rangle \left\langle 1\right| = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}
\]
Thus,
\[
\rho = \frac{1}{2}\left(\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\right) = \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{2}I

Comparing this with the general form \(\rho = \frac{1}{2}\left(I + \vec{r} \cdot \vec{\sigma}\right)\), we see that \(\vec{r} \cdot \vec{\sigma} = 0\), which implies that \(\vec{r} = (0, 0, 0)\) because there are no components of \(\vec{r}\) contributing in the \(x\), \(y\), or \(z\) directions.

Therefore, the geometrical position of the given density matrix in the qubit space is at the origin of the Bloch sphere.
